solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Shipmaster fine after eclipse cheers part of UK, Westward Ho! (7,4)

indicatorNotes.Westward: an across entry reads west to east, so heading westward means travelling right to left, turning NI round
indicatorNotes.after: 'fine after' the rest puts OK at the very end, behind everything that comes before it

blocks.note: to cap is to outdo or eclipse

annotation.surface: A cry of 'Westward Ho!' as a ship sets out west, borrowing the title of the Devon novel and village.
annotation.walkthrough: Split the name into small chunks and the long cheerful surface falls apart; 'fine after' means OK comes last of all.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the pirate captain of the Jolly Roger in Peter Pan is a shipmaster.

entries.clue: Bit mean (7)

blocks.note: a noun: a piece snipped off, from a plant or a newspaper
an adjective: hurtful, as a remark can be

annotation.walkthrough: Both words look like verbs or a phrase ('a bit mean'), but one is a noun and the other an adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: Two plain senses: a snipped-off piece of a plant or newspaper, and wounding in the way an unkind remark is.

entries.clue: Introductions for this writer, up first to speak (6)

indicatorNotes.up: in a down entry, up means read bottom to top, so ME turns over
indicatorNotes.first: 'first to speak' is the opening letter of the word speak

blocks.note: this writer = ME, the setter, turned upward

annotation.surface: A writer asks to be allowed to speak first when introductions are made.
annotation.walkthrough: 'This writer' is the setter referring to themself: ME.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain but literary synonym: a proem is a preface to a book or speech.

entries.clue: Banter like silly kid (5-5)

indicatorNotes.silly: silly letters behave foolishly and will not stay in their given order

annotation.surface: Someone trades jokes like a daft child.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Like' looks like a comparison joining the halves, but it is fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal slang: a toddler is at ankle height, so a small kid is jokingly called this.

entries.clue: Loud guide from the south causing a stink (4)

indicatorNotes.from the south: in a down entry, starting from the south means reading from the bottom upward

blocks.note: a fin steers a fish, a surfboard or a rocket

annotation.surface: A noisy tour guide from the south of the country makes a stink.
annotation.walkthrough: FFIN is written upward to fill the light.
annotation.definitionFit: British slang: a niff is a bad smell.

entries.clue: Utterly dominate game, Chelsea full backs ultimately making mistakes (3,5)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: ultimately means in the end, so take each word's final letter

blocks.note: to own an opponent is slang for thrashing them
last letters of chelseA, fulL, backS

annotation.surface: A football report: Chelsea's full backs keep erring while the team dominates.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Full backs' is a football position, but here 'full' and 'backs' are just two words giving their last letters. Chelsea is a London football club.
annotation.definitionFit: Figurative use: scoring into your own net is the classic football blunder, and the phrase now means any self-inflicted mistake.

entries.clue: Taxing financial gain (7)

blocks.note: an adjective: exhausting, as a steep climb is
a noun: a big profit, as in 'make a ___'

annotation.walkthrough: Read together, 'taxing financial gain' sounds like a tax policy; split it after 'Taxing'.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: informally exhausting, and the idiom for a sudden large profit.

entries.clue: Having gone into herd, animal doctor misses opening in horse’s joint (7)

indicatorNotes.Having gone into: the shortened VET has gone into the herd word, so it sits inside FLOCK
indicatorNotes.misses opening: the opening of a word is its first letter, which VET misses

blocks.note: a flock is a herd of sheep or goats

annotation.surface: A vet goes into the herd and fails to spot a problem with a horse's leg.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Opening' is not a gap in a joint but the first letter of VET.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain anatomy: the joint just above a horse's hoof, with its tuft of hair.

entries.clue: Female set Down clue, originally camouflaged to describe Liberal hippy (6,5)

indicatorNotes.originally: originally means at the start, so only the clue's first letter is used
indicatorNotes.to describe: to describe a circle is to draw round it, so HID goes round L

blocks.note: to lower is to set down

annotation.surface: A woman writes a Down clue, disguising it to describe a liberal hippy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Down clue' tempts you to look at the grid; it is really LOWER then C.
annotation.definitionFit: A synonym from the 1960s, when hippies wore flowers as symbols of peace.

entries.clue: Maybe loyal group of Rowling readers occasionally fear the end for Cormoran Strike (3,4)

annotation.definition: Maybe loyal group of Rowling readers

indicatorNotes.occasionally: occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter of fear shows up
indicatorNotes.the end for: the end of Cormoran is its last letter

blocks.note: odd letters F, A of fear

annotation.surface: J.K. Rowling's readers fear the fate of her detective Cormoran Strike.
annotation.walkthrough: Cormoran Strike is Rowling's detective (written as Robert Galbraith), so 'Strike' reads as a name; here it is a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example, flagged by 'Maybe': devoted readers of one author form an organised following.

entries.clue: I put notices up for Spooner, yet quarrel (11)

annotation.definitionNote: the definition is the person speaking about their job; the answer is the noun for that person

indicatorNotes.for Spooner: Rev. Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of words, so his version of the phrase swaps them

blocks.note: yet = still; it gives up its ST sound and takes the B
quarrel = bicker; it hands over its B and collects the ST

annotation.surface: A man pins up notices yet still argues.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'I' is the person being defined, talking about their job.
annotation.definitionFit: A bill is a posted notice, and the person who pastes them on walls describes their work this way.

entries.clue: Arresting European suspect, impound drug smoked here (5,3)

indicatorNotes.Arresting: to arrest is to hold, so the jumbled word holds E inside it
indicatorNotes.suspect: suspect letters are dubious, not to be trusted in their given order

annotation.surface: Police arrest a European suspect and seize his drugs.
annotation.walkthrough: E slips between the D and N of the jumbled IMPOUND. 'Suspect' is a noun in the surface and the anagram signal in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the drug is named in the answer's first word, and a den is the place where it is smoked.

entries.clue: Gathering agents must infiltrate mostly unescorted? (6)

indicatorNotes.must infiltrate: agents infiltrate by getting inside, so CIA goes inside the other word
indicatorNotes.mostly: mostly means most but not all, so SOLO loses its last letter

annotation.surface: Spies must slip into a party where people have come without partners.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gathering' looks like a verb (collecting agents), but it is a noun: a party.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain noun synonym: an informal get-together of a club or group.

entries.clue: One seen around bed and seat following one’s husband (6,4)

blocks.note: f. = following, as in page references

annotation.surface: Someone sits by the bed next to their husband.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bed' suggests a bedroom, but it is the sea bed.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: a fish that lives near the sea bed is one seen around it.

entries.clue: Part of cooked breakfast, say, extremely generous (4)

indicatorNotes.extremely: extremely points to the extremes of the word, its outermost letters

annotation.surface: A generous serving as part of a fry-up.
annotation.walkthrough: A cooked breakfast is the British fry-up of bacon, sausage, toast and so on.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: fried or scrambled, they are one standard item on the plate.

entries.clue: Ignores the wishes of stupid boss, idle git wasting time (10)

indicatorNotes.stupid: stupid letters behave foolishly and will not stay in their given order
indicatorNotes.wasting: wasting means losing, so GIT loses T, the abbreviation for time

annotation.surface: A lazy boss is ignored by his staff.
annotation.walkthrough: A git is British slang for an unpleasant or foolish person.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to refuse someone the favour or compliance they want.

entries.clue: Undone by pressure, a bowler playing poorly (5,3)

indicatorNotes.Undone: something undone has been taken apart, so the letters are rebuilt in a new order

annotation.surface: A cricket bowler cracks under pressure and bowls badly.
annotation.walkthrough: In cricket the bowler delivers the ball; here the word is just letters.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom from golf: scoring worse than the standard means performing under your usual form.

entries.clue: Here, secured by sailor on bow of clipper, is one of two anchors? (10)

indicatorNotes.secured by: something secured by a sailor is held in their grip, so PRESENT sits inside OS
indicatorNotes.bow of: the bow is the front of a ship, so the first letter of clipper
indicatorNotes.on: in an across entry, the rest is placed on C, coming after it

annotation.surface: A sailor on a clipper ship secures one of its two anchors.
annotation.walkthrough: The anchors are not a ship's but a news programme's presenters, which the question mark signals.
annotation.definitionFit: A pun on anchor, the presenter of a broadcast: sharing that role with one other person.

entries.clue: Quiet pal so excited about rook in trees (7)

indicatorNotes.excited: excited letters are stirred up out of their order
indicatorNotes.about: about means around, so the jumbled letters go round R

annotation.surface: A quiet friend gets excited about a rook nesting in the trees.
annotation.walkthrough: The rook is not the bird in the trees but R from chess.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: tall, fast-growing trees of the willow family.

entries.clue: Case online tuition covers (4)

indicatorNotes.covers: the phrase covers, or contains, the answer inside it

annotation.surface: A legal case about online teaching.
annotation.walkthrough: The word is a crossword favourite, from French, for a small ornamental holder.
annotation.definitionFit: A specific kind of case: a small decorative one for needles, pins or cosmetics.

entries.clue: Firm to accommodate working after dark very soon? (7)

indicatorNotes.to accommodate: to accommodate a guest is to take them in, so TIGHT takes ON inside

annotation.surface: A firm takes on extra work in the evening to be ready soon.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Firm' reads as a company; it is an adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description, marked by '?': the coming evening is both after dark and not far off.

entries.clue: Prior to game of chance, lid of Biro is under the table (6)

indicatorNotes.Prior to: prior to means before, so B is placed ahead of the game
indicatorNotes.lid of: the lid sits on top, so the first letter in a down entry

blocks.note: lotto, a lottery or bingo-like game

annotation.surface: Before the lottery draw, the cap of a pen has fallen under the table.
annotation.walkthrough: A Biro is a ballpoint pen. 'Under the table' is the drunk's position, not the pen lid's.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: someone who has drunk so much they slide off their chair is very drunk.

entries.clue: Ad-lib technique in rally cut short (6)

indicatorNotes.cut short: a word cut short has had its tail trimmed, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: IMPROVE (to rally, recover) without its E

annotation.surface: A political rally is cut short and speakers have to ad-lib.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rally' is a verb: a patient who rallies gets better.
annotation.definitionFit: Short for improvisation: performing unscripted, making it up on the spot.

entries.clue: Author Deighton’s visiting Omsk, busy Russian city (8)

indicatorNotes.visiting: a visitor goes into a place, so LENS goes into the other letters
indicatorNotes.busy: busy letters are bustling about out of their order

annotation.surface: Len Deighton visits two Russian cities, Omsk being lively.
annotation.walkthrough: Omsk is a real Russian city, so it looks like the definition; it is fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: an old city on the Dnieper in western Russia.

entries.clue: Sudden shot (4)

blocks.note: an adjective: done on the spur of the moment, as an election can be

annotation.walkthrough: 'Sudden shot' reads as a gunshot; split it into an adjective and a photo.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: informally, sudden or hurried, and a casual photograph.

entries.clue: Poker Face, absolutely rubbish (7)

blocks.note: dead = absolutely, as in dead right
to pan is to rubbish, criticise harshly

annotation.surface: A reviewer calls the song Poker Face absolutely rubbish.
annotation.walkthrough: The capitals point to the Lady Gaga song, but the definition is simply an expressionless face.
annotation.definitionFit: A synonym phrase: a face that gives nothing away, as a card player's must.

entries.clue: Figure Italian team will include Angelo in the middle (7)

indicatorNotes.will include: to include is to take in, so INTER takes GE inside it
indicatorNotes.in the middle: Angelo in the middle is just its central letters

annotation.surface: An Italian football team signs a player called Angelo to play in midfield.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Figure' could be a shape or a person; here it is a number.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain mathematical sense: a whole number is a figure.

entries.clue: Ailment cheeky son lies about? That catches relative out for starters (5,6)

indicatorNotes.lies about: about means turned round, so the cheeky son lies facing the other way
indicatorNotes.catches: to catch is to hold, so THAT holds RO inside it
indicatorNotes.for starters: starters come first, so take the first letter of each word

annotation.surface: A cheeky son fakes an illness to skip school, until a relative catches him out.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark ends the first half, but the second half is still wordplay: 'That' is not a pointer back but letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a sore throat caused by streptococcus bacteria is one ailment.
